idiom_name: mixin class expressions: (Base) => class extends Base {}
implementation_notes: The handbook's answer to 'we want the behaviour of multiple classes' is the mixin class pattern: a function constrained to a constructor type (type Constructor = new (...args: any[]) => {}) returns a class expression extending the base it was given, so the composed class has both sets of members and only one prototype chain - the handbook shows exactly the Scale(Sprite) shape, and MDN states the underlying constraint: 'A class can only have a single superclass, so multiple inheritance from tooling classes, for example, is not possible. The functionality must be provided by the superclass'. What still requires the classic twin pair: two parents that each own state and a constructor, because a mixin must forward all constructor arguments through a single rest parameter, and two incompatible constructor signatures cannot be combined. Use the pair there, with the reference typed as the other class and cleared on teardown.
pitfalls: Mixins may not declare private or protected members (stated in the handbook); use ECMAScript private fields (#x), which stay outside the mixin's structural type.

A mixin class must forward all constructor arguments with one rest parameter (constructor(...args: any[]) { super(...args); }), so two mixins with different constructor signatures cannot both be applied meaningfully and those arguments are not type-checked.
Applying two mixins with a member of the same name produces an intersection type whose runtime behaviour follows the last application while the type claims both - the mismatch is silent.
A mixin-composed class is not a subclass of its mixins, so instanceof narrowing cannot see the composed capability; use structural checks or Symbol.hasInstance.

variants.name: Classic twin pair (two classes with mutual references)
variants.idiom_name: two classes with mutual references (classic Twin, for stateful parents)
variants.implementation_notes: When both parents own state and a constructor, no mixin can compose them: write one class per parent, give each a reference typed as its partner, create the pair in one factory function and return the end the caller needs. In TypeScript the link is a plain property - private and readonly are erased at runtime, so they document intent but provide no protection - so keep both classes in one module and never publish the partner through a public accessor.
pitfalls: private and readonly are compile-time only: any JavaScript caller can re-link or read a published twin property at runtime.
Definite-assignment assertions (!) hide the pair invariant from the type system - an unlinked instance compiles and fails on the first click.
Class fields are initialised in declaration order and after super(), so a twin reference captured during base-class construction is still undefined.
Serialising either end (JSON.stringify, structuredClone) either throws on the circular structure or silently drops the link, leaving the other side holding a broken pair.
